title: Chapter 9 Drill: Surgical Oncology, Skin, Soft Tissue, and Plastic Surgery

items.stem: A 45-year-old man presents with a swollen finger held in flexion, pain on passive extension along the whole finger, tenderness along the flexor sheath, and fusiform swelling. Which diagnosis requires urgent surgical drainage?
options: Felon of the fingertip pulp
Pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis
Paronychia limited to the nail fold
Herpetic whitlow of the distal phalanx
items.explanation: Kanavel signs of flexor sheath infection are a flexed posture, fusiform swelling, flexor sheath tenderness, and pain with passive extension. Delay risks tendon necrosis and spread to deep spaces, so irrigation or drainage with antibiotics is urgent. A felon is a closed pulp space infection. Paronychia stays at the nail fold. Herpetic whitlow is viral and drainage worsens it.

items.stem: A 66-year-old woman is on a checkpoint inhibitor for metastatic melanoma. In week 8 she develops six watery stools daily, abdominal cramping, and mild fever. Stool cultures are negative. What is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Hold the drug and start corticosteroids for immune colitis
Continue the drug and give loperamide alone
Start empiric oral vancomycin for Clostridioides difficile and continue the drug unchanged and continue the drug unchanged
Arrange urgent total colectomy
items.explanation: Checkpoint inhibitors cause immune-mediated colitis, graded by stool frequency, and moderate or higher grades need the drug held and corticosteroids started. Loperamide alone masks progression. Negative cultures and a drug exposure make infection less likely, so empiric antibiotics are not the first move. Colectomy is reserved for perforation or disease refractory to steroids and biologic therapy, not for a first presentation.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman with familial adenomatous polyposis after colectomy now has a firm, enlarging abdominal wall mass. Biopsy shows bland fibroblastic cells with beta-catenin mutation and no metastatic potential. What is the best initial approach?
options: Immediate wide resection with margins of 5 cm and adjacent muscle
Adjuvant anthracycline chemotherapy
Active surveillance or systemic therapy, as surgery often triggers regrowth
Whole abdominal radiation
items.explanation: Desmoid tumors are locally aggressive but do not metastasize, and they commonly follow abdominal surgery in patients with familial polyposis. Many stabilize or regress, so surveillance is first line, and systemic agents are used for progression. Radical resection often provokes recurrence. Anthracycline regimens are reserved for refractory cases. Abdominal radiation risks bowel injury and is not routine.

items.stem: A 57-year-old man has a chronic nonhealing ulcer that has developed within an old burn scar on the leg over 25 years. Biopsy shows invasive squamous cell carcinoma. What is the most appropriate description of this entity and its behavior?
options: Pyoderma gangrenosum, an inflammatory ulcer that responds to systemic corticosteroids and immunosuppression
Keratoacanthoma, which regresses without treatment
Bowen disease, which never invades beyond the epidermis
Marjolin ulcer, which tends to metastasize more often than ordinary sun-related squamous carcinoma
items.explanation: Squamous carcinoma arising in a chronic scar or wound is a Marjolin ulcer, a disease with a higher metastatic rate and a worse prognosis than ordinary actinic squamous carcinoma. Pyoderma gangrenosum is an inflammatory ulcer, and biopsy would not show invasive carcinoma. Keratoacanthoma is a rapidly growing, self-limited lesion. Bowen disease is in situ squamous carcinoma and by definition is not invasive.

items.stem: A 24-year-old man has a painless 3 cm left supraclavicular node, night sweats, and weight loss. Needle aspiration was nondiagnostic. What is the next best step?
options: Excisional node biopsy to preserve architecture
Repeat fine needle aspiration in two weeks and wait for a cytology result before further steps
Empiric course of oral antibiotics for four weeks
Radical neck dissection
items.explanation: Suspected lymphoma needs an intact node so pathologists can assess architecture and immunophenotype, which an excisional biopsy provides. Repeating aspiration is again likely to be nondiagnostic. Antibiotics delay diagnosis in a patient with B symptoms and a persistent node. A neck dissection is a major cancer operation that is unjustified before a diagnosis is established.

items.stem: Which phase of the cell cycle is the most sensitive to ionizing radiation, and why does fractionated dosing take advantage of this?
options: Early S phase, because DNA repair is absent during synthesis and cells cannot recover and cells cannot recover
Late G2 and mitosis, because cells redistribute into these sensitive phases between fractions
Early G1, because cells cannot arrest at any checkpoint
G0 resting cells, because they divide rapidly after injury
items.explanation: Cells in late G2 and mitosis are the most radiosensitive, while late S phase is relatively resistant. Fractionation lets surviving cells redistribute into sensitive phases, lets normal tissue repair, and allows reoxygenation of hypoxic tumor. Early S phase and G1 are not the peak of sensitivity. Resting G0 cells are the most resistant, since they are not dividing and tolerate damage best.

items.stem: A 61-year-old man is receiving systemic therapy for metastatic cancer. Baseline imaging showed a liver lesion of 40 mm. After three months it measures 26 mm, with no new lesions and no change in other target lesions. By standard response criteria, how is this response classified?
options: Complete response, because the lesion has clearly shrunk and no new lesions have appeared and no new lesions have appeared
Stable disease, because new lesions have not appeared
Partial response, because the target sum fell 30 percent or more
Progressive disease, because the lesion is still measurable
items.explanation: Under RECIST, partial response means at least a 30 percent decrease in the sum of target lesion diameters. Here the fall is 35 percent. Complete response requires disappearance of all target lesions, so measurable residual disease excludes it. Stable disease applies when shrinkage is under 30 percent and growth is under 20 percent. Progression needs at least a 20 percent increase or new lesions, neither of which occurred.

items.stem: A 72-year-old man with lung cancer has a large right pleural effusion and recurrent dyspnea. After thoracentesis the lung expands fully and symptoms resolve, but fluid reaccumulates in one week. Which option offers durable symptom control?
options: Indwelling tunneled pleural catheter or pleurodesis
Repeat thoracentesis every week indefinitely
Surgical decortication with lung resection
Diuretic therapy for the effusion
items.explanation: A malignant effusion with a lung that fully re-expands is a good candidate for pleurodesis or an indwelling catheter, which allows home drainage. Repeated thoracentesis is burdensome and risks pneumothorax and empyema. Decortication is for a trapped lung and is too major here. Diuretics do not control exudative malignant effusions that arise from pleural tumor involvement.

items.stem: A 60-year-old man has a 22 cm retroperitoneal mass displacing the right kidney, with fat density and fine calcifications on imaging. Which statement about operative management is most accurate?
options: Enucleation along the pseudocapsule is adequate
Complete en bloc resection with adjacent involved organs gives the best control
Neoadjuvant chemotherapy should always precede surgery
Debulking should be avoided because local recurrence does not change survival in this tumor type
items.explanation: Well-differentiated or dedifferentiated liposarcoma is the usual retroperitoneal fat-density mass, and complete resection with adjacent organs such as the kidney or colon is the main curative strategy. Enucleation leaves microscopic disease and causes early recurrence. Chemotherapy has limited activity in these subtypes and is not mandatory first. Local recurrence is the dominant cause of death, so complete resection matters.

items.stem: A 64-year-old farmer has a pearly, ulcerated nodule on the nasolabial fold, biopsied as morpheaform basal cell carcinoma. Which approach offers the highest cure rate while preserving facial tissue?
options: Standard excision with a 2 mm margin in the clinic
Curettage and electrodesiccation of the lesion
Cryotherapy repeated at monthly intervals
Mohs micrographic surgery with complete margin assessment
items.explanation: Morpheaform tumors on the central face are high-risk, with subclinical extension that is hard to see. Mohs surgery examines the entire margin, giving the best cure with maximal tissue sparing. A narrow standard excision risks positive margins. Curettage and cryotherapy suit small, low-risk, well-defined lesions on the trunk and limbs, not infiltrative lesions in a high-recurrence facial zone.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man with metastatic colorectal cancer is considered for cetuximab. Which tumor finding would predict that this drug will not work?
options: Overexpression of CEA in the serum, which only tracks tumor burden in this setting, which only tracks tumor burden in this setting
Mutation in KRAS, which keeps the pathway active downstream
Microsatellite stability on mismatch repair testing
Liver as the only site of metastasis
items.explanation: Cetuximab blocks the epidermal growth factor receptor, but a KRAS or NRAS mutation activates signaling downstream of the receptor, so blockade is bypassed. Treatment is therefore limited to RAS wild-type tumors. A high CEA level only reflects tumor burden. Microsatellite stability does not predict anti-receptor resistance. Isolated liver disease may still respond and may even become resectable after effective therapy.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman has a 5 cm gastric submucosal mass with spindle cells, positive for KIT and DOG1. Which therapy would be added to resection for a high-risk tumor?
options: Adjuvant cisplatin and doxorubicin for a fixed number of cycles
Adjuvant pelvic radiation
Adjuvant tamoxifen
Adjuvant imatinib for a defined period
items.explanation: Gastrointestinal stromal tumors are driven by KIT or PDGFRA mutations and respond to tyrosine kinase inhibition. High-risk resected tumors, judged by size, mitotic rate, and site, receive adjuvant imatinib. Conventional cytotoxic chemotherapy has little benefit. Radiation has no routine role in gastric disease, and hormone therapy has no target in these tumors. Only tyrosine kinase inhibition matches the mutation.

items.stem: A 71-year-old man has a slowly enlarging irregular tan macule on the cheek, with a biopsy showing atypical melanocytes along the basal layer without invasion. Surgery is considered high risk because of comorbidities. Which nonoperative option is reasonable?
options: Topical imiquimod or radiation for lentigo maligna
Systemic checkpoint inhibitor therapy
Topical fluorouracil for three days then discharge
Sentinel node biopsy followed by clinical observation
items.explanation: Lentigo maligna is melanoma in situ on chronically sun-damaged skin. When surgery is unsuitable, imiquimod or radiotherapy can be used, although recurrence is higher than with excision. Checkpoint inhibitors are for advanced invasive disease. Brief fluorouracil is for actinic keratoses, not melanoma. Sentinel biopsy is not indicated for in situ disease because nodal spread does not occur.

items.stem: A 7-year-old girl needs a groin wound closed after tumor excision, and the wound bed is clean and well vascularized but too large for primary closure. Which graft type has the greatest tendency to contract but the highest take rate in this setting?
options: Full-thickness skin graft
Composite graft with cartilage
Split-thickness skin graft
Pedicled muscle flap
items.explanation: Split-thickness grafts include epidermis and part of the dermis, take reliably on a clean bed, and heal donor sites quickly, but contract more than thicker grafts. A full-thickness graft contracts less and suits the face and hands, but takes less reliably and is limited by donor size. Composite grafts have the poorest take. A flap brings its own blood supply and is unnecessary for a healthy wound bed.

items.stem: A 66-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer has nausea, constipation, confusion, polyuria, and a serum calcium of 14.2 mg/dL after correction for albumin. What is the best initial treatment?
options: Intravenous fluid followed by a bisphosphonate such as zoledronic acid
Furosemide alone without fluids, since diuresis lowers the calcium quickly
Oral calcium restriction as sole therapy
Intravenous calcium gluconate to stabilize membranes
items.explanation: Hypercalcemia of malignancy causes volume depletion, so hydration comes first, then a bisphosphonate to inhibit osteoclast resorption, with denosumab for refractory cases. Loop diuretics are used only after volume repletion and not alone. Dietary restriction barely affects malignant bone resorption. Giving calcium worsens the disorder, since the problem is excess calcium rather than deficiency. Fluids and the bone-directed drug address the actual mechanism.

items.stem: A 47-year-old man begins chemotherapy for bulky high-grade lymphoma. Twelve hours later his potassium is high, phosphate is high, calcium is low, uric acid is elevated, and creatinine is rising. What is the best next step in management?
options: Calcium infusion to correct the low calcium
Isotonic hydration with a uric acid lowering agent and monitoring
Urinary alkalinization with sodium bicarbonate alone
Withholding fluids to avoid pulmonary edema
items.explanation: This is tumor lysis syndrome. Treatment centers on vigorous hydration to maintain urine output, a xanthine oxidase inhibitor or rasburicase to lower uric acid, and monitoring for arrhythmia with treatment of hyperkalemia. Calcium is given only for symptoms or arrhythmia, because it can precipitate with phosphate. Alkalinization alone is no longer favored, and fluid restriction worsens kidney injury.

items.stem: A 33-year-old mechanic injects grease into his index finger from a high-pressure gun. The finger looks only mildly swollen with a tiny puncture wound and little pain. What is the best management?
options: Reassurance and oral analgesics at home
Tetanus booster and a splint with early follow-up
Warm soaks and a short course of oral antibiotics
Urgent surgical exploration and wide debridement
items.explanation: High-pressure injection injuries look deceptively benign but spread material along tendon sheaths and cause ischemia, inflammation, and necrosis, so early wide debridement reduces amputation rates. Reassurance and soaks delay care. Tetanus and a splint are appropriate additions but do not remove the injected material. Antibiotics without debridement leave the toxic substance in place. Early exploration is what saves the digit.

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman with a long history of breast cancer treated by axillary dissection and radiation reports a heavy, swollen right arm with pitting early and nonpitting later. Which measure forms the foundation of treatment?
options: Long-term loop diuretics, since they remove protein-rich fluid from the limb
Routine liposuction in all patients
Complex decongestive therapy with compression, manual drainage, and exercise
Prolonged arm elevation with no compression
items.explanation: Lymphedema is protein-rich fluid accumulation from lymphatic injury, and its core treatment is decongestive therapy combining compression garments, manual lymphatic drainage, skin care, and exercise. Diuretics remove water but not protein and are ineffective. Liposuction suits late fatty change in selected patients, not everyone. Elevation alone is insufficient and does not prevent progression. Garments and exercise maintain the reduction once achieved.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man with advanced pancreatic cancer reports severe constant upper abdominal pain radiating to the back, poorly controlled by acetaminophen. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Start an opioid with a bowel regimen and consider celiac plexus neurolysis
Add only a nonsteroidal drug and reassess in a month
Delay opioids until pain is intolerable to avoid dependence
Prescribe an opioid with no laxative to avoid bloating
items.explanation: Cancer pain follows the stepwise ladder, and severe pain warrants opioids dosed on a schedule with breakthrough doses. Opioid constipation is predictable, so a bowel regimen starts at the same time. Celiac plexus neurolysis is effective for pancreatic pain. An anti-inflammatory alone is inadequate for severe pain, and withholding opioids for fear of dependence is inappropriate in terminal illness.

items.stem: A 44-year-old woman has colon cancer diagnosed at 41. Her father had endometrial cancer at 50, and her paternal aunt had colon cancer at 46. Tumor testing shows loss of MSH2 and MSH6 staining. Which statement best describes the underlying defect?
options: A germline APC mutation that causes hundreds of colonic adenomas and near-certain cancer by midlife and near-certain cancer by midlife
A germline STK11 mutation that causes hamartomatous polyps
A germline mismatch repair gene mutation that causes microsatellite instability
A somatic BRAF mutation that causes sporadic methylation of MLH1
items.explanation: Lynch syndrome results from a germline mismatch repair mutation, so errors in short repeated sequences accumulate and tumors show microsatellite instability. Loss of MSH2 with MSH6 points to a germline defect in that gene pair. APC mutation produces a florid polyposis phenotype that is absent here. STK11 causes Peutz-Jeghers syndrome. BRAF mutation with MLH1 methylation indicates a sporadic tumor and does not explain this family pattern.

items.stem: A 73-year-old woman has a rapidly growing, painless, firm red nodule on her forearm. Biopsy shows small round blue cells with perinuclear dot-like staining for cytokeratin 20. Which tumor is this, and which risk factor is typical?
options: Basal cell carcinoma, associated with arsenic exposure and a nested palisaded growth pattern in the dermis
Merkel cell carcinoma, associated with polyomavirus infection and ultraviolet exposure
Amelanotic melanoma, associated with a prior congenital nevus
Cutaneous lymphoma, associated with chronic scar injury
items.explanation: Merkel cell carcinoma is an aggressive neuroendocrine skin tumor, linked to Merkel cell polyomavirus, sun exposure, age, and immunosuppression, and it stains for cytokeratin 20 in a perinuclear dot pattern. Basal cell carcinoma does not show small round blue cells with that stain. Melanoma stains for S100 and SOX10. Cutaneous lymphoma stains for lymphoid markers and not this pattern.

items.stem: A 78-year-old bedbound man has a sacral pressure injury exposing bone with undermined edges, purulent drainage, and fever. Probing reaches rough bone, and inflammatory markers are elevated. Which management is most appropriate?
options: Moist dressings alone and daily whirlpool
Immediate rotational flap over the unprepared wound
Topical antibiotic ointment, a hydrocolloid dressing, and continued supine positioning
Surgical debridement with bone biopsy, antibiotics, offloading, and nutrition, before flap coverage
items.explanation: A stage 4 injury with osteomyelitis needs debridement of necrotic tissue and infected bone, culture-directed antibiotics, pressure relief, and nutritional optimization, and flap coverage follows once the wound is clean. Dressings alone cannot treat bone infection. Covering an infected, unprepared wound with a flap will fail. Ointment with continued pressure leaves the cause untreated. Each step addresses a part of the disease.

items.stem: A surgeon plans to cover an exposed tibia after open fracture debridement with a rotated gastrocnemius muscle based on its dominant pedicle. How is this tissue transfer best classified?
options: A local pedicled muscle flap
A free tissue transfer requiring microsurgical anastomosis
A full-thickness skin graft
A tissue expander reconstruction
items.explanation: A muscle that stays attached to its own dominant blood supply and rotates into the defect is a pedicled flap, and a local one when used near the donor site. A free flap is detached and reconnected by microsurgery. A skin graft has no blood supply of its own. Expansion stretches adjacent skin over time rather than transposing muscle.

items.stem: A 54-year-old man has a 12 cm painless thigh mass that is soft on examination. MRI shows internal thick septa and nodular nonfat components. Which test best distinguishes lipoma from well-differentiated liposarcoma?
options: Serum alpha-fetoprotein level
MDM2 amplification on tissue testing
Fluorodeoxyglucose uptake alone
Presence of a thin capsule on ultrasound
items.explanation: Well-differentiated liposarcoma carries amplification of the MDM2 gene, detected by fluorescence in situ hybridization, which separates it from benign lipoma. Alpha-fetoprotein is not a sarcoma marker. Metabolic uptake overlaps between the entities. A thin capsule is seen in both. Deep location, large size, and septa are also warning features that warrant tissue diagnosis before surgery.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman has a 1.2 mm thick melanoma on the calf, nonulcerated, with no palpable nodes and negative staging imaging. Her sentinel node biopsy shows a 0.4 mm micrometastasis. What is the most appropriate nodal management according to current evidence?
options: Immediate completion lymph node dissection of the groin, because any positive sentinel node mandates it
Elective dissection of the contralateral groin
Nodal ultrasound surveillance and consideration of adjuvant systemic therapy
Observation only because the node focus is under 1 mm
items.explanation: A positive sentinel node upstages disease to stage III. Trials of completion dissection showed no melanoma-specific survival gain, so ultrasound surveillance is standard, and adjuvant immunotherapy or targeted therapy is considered. Contralateral dissection has no role. Observation alone ignores the stage III risk, since even small nodal deposits are an indication for adjuvant discussion. Surveillance and adjuvant discussion are the evidence-based path.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man with rectal cancer has three resectable metastases confined to the right lobe of the liver, stable disease on chemotherapy, and no extrahepatic disease. Which statement best supports operative therapy?
options: Hepatic metastases always indicate incurable systemic disease
Liver resection is contraindicated when more than one lesion is present
Radiation of the primary alone is enough for liver disease
Complete resection of metastases with adequate remnant liver can provide long-term survival
items.explanation: In selected colorectal cancer patients, complete resection or ablation of limited liver metastases with sufficient remnant liver offers long-term survival and some cure, which is the oligometastatic concept. Calling it always incurable ignores that data. Multiple lesions are acceptable when resection is complete. Pelvic radiation does not treat established hepatic metastases. Patient selection by remnant liver volume is essential.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man has a 2.3 mm thick melanoma on the back with no ulceration and clinically negative nodes. After wide excision planning, which surgical margin from the biopsy scar is recommended?
options: 0.5 cm, with fascia removed
2 cm, with fascia preserved
5 cm, with underlying muscle removed
1 mm, with margin control by frozen section
items.explanation: Randomized trials support a 2 cm margin for melanomas thicker than 2 mm, and 1 to 2 cm for those 1 to 2 mm thick, with fascia generally preserved. Margins of 0.5 cm suit in situ disease. Wider margins such as 5 cm showed no survival benefit and add morbidity. Frozen section margin control is used for lentigo maligna type lesions in special sites, not for a standard invasive trunk melanoma.

items.stem: A 55-year-old woman receiving fluorouracil for colon cancer develops severe mucositis, profound neutropenia, and diarrhea within days of her first cycle. Which inherited deficiency most likely explains this?
options: Dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase deficiency, which impairs drug clearance
Thiopurine methyltransferase deficiency, which impairs drug clearance
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, which causes hemolysis
Uridine diphosphate glucuronosyltransferase deficiency affecting irinotecan
items.explanation: Dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase breaks down most of a fluorouracil dose, so a deficiency causes drug accumulation and early, severe toxicity. Thiopurine methyltransferase governs mercaptopurine and azathioprine handling. G6PD deficiency causes oxidant-triggered hemolysis, not mucositis. The UGT1A1 variant increases SN-38 exposure and toxicity from irinotecan, a different drug, so it does not fit a fluorouracil-only regimen. Check fluorouracil exposure when toxicity appears so early.

items.stem: On postoperative day 1 after a free flap breast reconstruction, the flap becomes dusky purple and tense, with brisk dark bleeding on pinprick and rapid capillary refill. What is the most likely problem and best next step?
options: Arterial insufficiency, so observe overnight
Normal reperfusion, so elevate the area and watch
Venous congestion, so return urgently to the operating room to explore
Infection, so start antibiotics only
items.explanation: A purple, swollen flap with brisk dark bleeding and fast refill is the classic sign of venous outflow obstruction, which is a surgical emergency because the flap can fail within hours. Arterial insufficiency appears pale, cool, and slow to bleed. Waiting wastes the salvage window. Infection does not cause this early picture, and antibiotics alone do not relieve a thrombosed vein.

items.stem: A 68-year-old woman with metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma develops a swollen left leg. Duplex imaging shows femoral vein thrombosis. Her creatinine clearance is normal and she has no bleeding. Which treatment is most appropriate?
options: An inferior vena cava filter alone
Aspirin for six months, since it treats established venous clot in cancer patients
Warfarin targeted to a very low INR
A direct oral anticoagulant such as apixaban for at least six months
items.explanation: Cancer-associated thrombosis is treated with therapeutic anticoagulation, and direct oral agents like apixaban are effective alternatives to injected formulations in patients without high gastrointestinal bleeding risk. A filter is reserved for those who cannot be anticoagulated. Aspirin does not adequately treat an established venous clot. Warfarin is less effective in malignancy and needs a standard therapeutic INR, not a low target.

items.stem: A 59-year-old woman with recurrent ovarian cancer has had three episodes of colicky pain and vomiting. CT shows multiple levels of small bowel obstruction with carcinomatosis. She wishes to be home. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Laparotomy with extensive bowel resection and anastomosis at each obstructed level
Medical palliation with antiemetics, antisecretory agents, and venting gastrostomy
Total parenteral nutrition as primary therapy
Endoscopic stent placement across all obstructed levels
items.explanation: Obstruction at several levels from carcinomatosis rarely is correctable, and surgery carries high morbidity with short survival. Antiemetics, octreotide, corticosteroids, and opioids control symptoms, and a venting gastrostomy lets her eat small amounts at home. Parenteral nutrition does not relieve obstruction and is not primary palliation. Stents are practical for a single focal site, not multiple levels.

items.stem: A 49-year-old woman has a deep, firm 8 cm thigh mass that has grown over four months. MRI suggests a soft tissue sarcoma. Which biopsy approach is best before any treatment?
options: Excisional biopsy through a transverse incision
Fine needle aspiration alone with cytology
Open incisional biopsy through an incision away from the future scar
Core needle biopsy placed along the planned resection axis
items.explanation: Core needle biopsy gives enough tissue for histology and grade, and the tract is positioned so it can be excised with the specimen. Excisional biopsy of a large mass contaminates tissue planes and compromises later resection. Fine needle cytology rarely gives reliable subtype and grade. An incision away from the planned incision seeds a second field that must be removed with the tumor.

items.stem: A 35-year-old man has a slowly growing, indurated violaceous plaque on the chest wall with finger-like extensions that recurred after a narrow excision. Biopsy shows storiform spindle cells positive for CD34. Which definitive approach is best?
options: Observation because metastases never occur
Systemic cytotoxic chemotherapy as first treatment
Wide local excision with negative margins or Mohs surgery
Another narrow excision with skin graft closure
items.explanation: Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans is a locally infiltrative tumor, CD34 positive, with the COL1A1 to PDGFB fusion, and recurrence follows inadequate margins. Wide excision or Mohs surgery with clear margins is standard. Distant metastasis is rare but possible, so observation is wrong. Chemotherapy is ineffective, though imatinib is used for unresectable disease. Repeating a narrow excision repeats the failure.

items.stem: A 29-year-old man has recurrent painful nodules, sinus tracts, and scarring in both axillae and the groin despite repeated antibiotics. The disease is Hurley stage 3 with interconnected tracts. Which operation is most appropriate?
options: Wide excision of affected skin and subcutaneous tissue with staged closure
Incision and drainage of each abscess alone, followed by long antibiotic courses
Unroofing of only the largest single tract
Antibiotics for a further year without surgery
items.explanation: Hidradenitis suppurativa that has progressed to extensive tracts and scarring needs wide excision of the diseased apocrine-bearing tissue to remove the reservoir of disease. Drainage of abscesses gives only short relief and recurrence is nearly universal. Unroofing one tract leaves others in place. Prolonged antibiotics do not cure advanced stage disease. Surgery addresses the disease reservoir.
